video_title: Rick Rule: Oil Is Going Higher In Coming Years, Making Oil Stocks CHEAP Right Now
gist: Rick Rule argues the 2026 oil price spike from resumed US-Iran hostilities is masking a deeper structural shortage from three decades of underinvestment, making oil majors (Exxon, Chevron, Occidental) and select Canadian producers cheap on a 2029-2030 view, while he also lays out uranium, Venezuela, and North Sea opportunities and a mixed take on government subsidies flooding into critical minerals and nuclear.

themes.theme: Structural oil shortage vs. the Iran-driven price spike

insights.claim: Rick Rule argues the 2026 rise in oil prices (Brent above $90 and approaching $94-95, WTI nearing $90) driven by resumed US-Iran hostilities reflects the threat of a shortage rather than an actual physical shortage, meaning prices would go much higher still if a real supply disruption materialized and had to be rationed by price.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Distinguishes a temporary geopolitical risk premium from a structural repricing, implying downside risk to oil prices if a ceasefire holds even as the longer-term structural case stays intact.
insights.quote: the increase in oil prices that we've seen is as a consequence of the threat of a shortage as opposed to an actual shortage.

insights.claim: Rule's core thesis is that today's oil price move is a preview of a genuine structural shortage he expects in late 2029/early 2030, caused by roughly three decades of underinvestment in oil supply plus several recent years of the industry deferring sustaining capital investment.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Sets a multi-year forward catalyst (2029-2030) for oil investors to underwrite positions against, independent of near-term geopolitical noise.
insights.quote: The point of this is that the price escalation that you've seen in oil in calendar 2026 is really a preview of things to come.

insights.claim: The war has worsened the structural oil shortage on two fronts: deferred sustaining capital investment across producing nations (roughly a billion dollars a day, per Rule) has increased, and physical infrastructure destroyed in the conflict (in Iran, UAE, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia) now needs costly repair on top of that deferred spending.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: War damage compounds rather than offsets the pre-existing underinvestment problem, reinforcing the 2029-2030 supply-shortfall thesis.
insights.quote: the deferral of a billion dollars a day in sustaining capital investments has been exacerbated a lot by the war... This exacerbates the circumstance in 2029. It doesn't ameliorate it.

insights.claim: Rule notes Iran uses drilling and completion technology roughly 20 years out of date (unlike sanctions-exempt Qatar, which shares the South Pars field and uses modern US technology), meaning Iran's production is structurally inefficient versus regional peers regardless of the ceasefire outcome.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Implies Iran, Mexico, and Venezuela all need major infrastructure resets before their production potential can be realized, a multi-year setup rather than a quick swing factor for global supply.
insights.quote: The Iranians like the Mexicans and the Venezuelans need a major reset of their infrastructure spending.

insights.claim: Rule expects that if diplomacy prevails and Middle East peace returns, oil prices would fall sharply, both because high prices have already destroyed demand in low-income countries (demand that would return) and because high prices have incentivized every non-sanctioned exporter worldwide to produce more.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A near-term bear case for oil prices that could coexist with the longer-dated structural bull case — investors should separate their 2026-2027 price view from their 2029-2030 view.
insights.quote: When the supply increases and the demand doesn't increase, we see a crater in price much like was much like we saw... during the COVID periods of time.

insights.claim: Rule's investing time frame for the oil thesis is specifically 2029-2030, on which basis he considers oil stocks "truly cheap" today, independent of what happens with near-term war/ceasefire dynamics.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Frames the entry point as attractive for patient, multi-year holders even though near-term price direction is genuinely uncertain.
insights.quote: I'm thinking right now about 2029 and 2030... If you look at that time frame, oil stocks are cheap. I mean really truly cheap.

insights.claim: For most investors who can't stomach volatility, Rule recommends simply buying and holding Exxon, citing its 20-30 year track record of intelligent capital allocation, maintained sustaining capital investment (unlike many peers), and a major discovery in Guyana large enough to move the needle even for a company Exxon's size.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A low-effort, high-conviction core holding recommendation for oil-sector beta with dividend reinvestment as the value driver.
insights.quote: buy Exxon... enjoy the market beta, just sit back and let wonderful things happen to your account over time.

insights.claim: For investors wanting slightly more risk than Exxon, Rule suggests Chevron; for those willing to take on balance-sheet risk, he points to Occidental Petroleum, noting Buffett's involvement and that today's entry price is below Buffett's average cost.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A risk-tiered oil-major framework; Occidental's balance sheet risk from the Anadarko acquisition has been partly de-risked by Buffett's ~$7B purchase of gathering/transmission assets, which reduces upside but also reduces financial risk.
insights.quote: if you're willing to take some balance sheet risk buy accidental petroleum you know Buffett had the courage to buy it maybe you do too

insights.claim: Rule expects the US natural gas glut to clear within about two to two-and-a-half years, favoring Devon Energy (which recently merged with Coterra to become the largest independent US gas producer) and Equitable (the key Marcellus Shale operator in the US Northeast).
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A specific, time-bound catalyst (gas glut resolution in 2-2.5 years) with named beneficiaries for investors seeking gas-price-driven alpha beyond oil majors.

insights.claim: Rule argues American and Canadian oil producers are increasingly becoming the world's preferred partners over the next decade because of superior technology and capital discipline, contrasting Exxon favorably with France's Total, which he characterizes as effectively an outsourced arm of the French state rather than a shareholder-focused company.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A geopolitical-alignment argument for structurally overweighting North American oil majors versus state-influenced European peers.
insights.quote: Total is basically an outsourced apparatus of the French state, not necessarily run for the benefit of shareholders.

insights.claim: Best risk/reward exposure to a global resumption of new oil project investment and deferred maintenance spending, in Rule's view, is the largest US oilfield services companies — Schlumberger, Halliburton, and Transocean (RIG) — even if they aren't the best pure stock performers.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Oilfield services offer diversified exposure to a global capex re-acceleration (Venezuela, Iran repair, Gulf states) without single-country political risk.

insights.claim: Rule's previously discussed "Magnificent 7" of Canadian oil and gas stocks dropped to six after Shell acquired ARC Resources — which he says was his favorite of the group.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: M&A is actively consolidating the small pool of investable Canadian pure-plays, a dynamic investors should track for further takeouts.
insights.quote: that number fell seven weeks ago when Shell decided to take over ARC, which was also my favorite.

insights.claim: Rule's remaining Canadian oil & gas favorites are Cenovus (cheap on any metric despite being, in his words, not a particularly good company), Canadian Natural Resources (near-diversified exposure across almost every Canadian play), Freehold Royalty (his top remaining pick), Tourmaline (the best-performing Canadian producer), and Birchcliff and Peyto (the two gas-centric Canadian names).
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A named, ranked shortlist of Canadian energy equities for investors seeking exposure beyond US majors.

insights.claim: Rule flags International Petroleum, a Lundin family-controlled heavy oil producer whose major capital investments are largely behind it and is "just starting to gush cash," as a special situation that could get an added boost if Canadian PM Carney and President Trump agree to debottleneck the Keystone pipeline, enabling more Canadian heavy oil sales to heavy-oil-starved US Gulf Coast refiners.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A small-cap (50,000 bbl/day) idiosyncratic cash-flow inflection story with a specific binary catalyst (Keystone debottlenecking) to monitor.

insights.claim: Rule flags Canadian PM Mark Carney as a real political risk for Canadian energy investors: unlike his predecessor, Carney understands oil and gas revenue funds his spending plans, but he remains fundamentally anti-hydrocarbon in stance.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Political-leadership risk is explicitly named as a headwind investors must price into any Canadian energy position, separate from the commodity thesis itself.
insights.quote: The headline political risk is that the guy who runs the place doesn't like you.

themes.theme: Venezuela and the Orinoco heavy-oil opportunity

insights.claim: Rule says Venezuela's current production surge (following Maduro's departure) is not driven by reinvestment but by overpulling existing producing wells, which he calls dangerous and unsustainable.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Warns investors not to mistake the current Venezuelan output rebound for a durable, well-managed production recovery.
insights.quote: The current production surge that you're seeing in Venezuela... isn't a function of reinvestment. It's a function of overpulling existing producing assets which is very dangerous.

insights.claim: Rule personally invested in Venezuelan oil exploration four separate times over his career and had four exploration successes on purely geological terms, but every one of those successes was subsequently nationalized by the Venezuelan government before he could fully monetize them.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A vivid, first-hand illustration of Venezuela's combination of world-class geology and extreme expropriation risk — the risk/reward tension any Venezuela-exposed investor must weigh.
insights.quote: based on geology, Venezuela is the most permissive terrain in my life... I've suffered four nationalizations, which is to say that every single exploration success was stolen from me.

insights.claim: Chevron, which stayed in Venezuela throughout the sanctions period rather than exiting, stands to benefit hugely from any Venezuelan reopening, according to Rule.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Chevron's decision to remain gives it a durable first-mover advantage versus competitors who exited, a differentiator for its Venezuela-linked upside relative to peers.

insights.claim: Rule estimates developing Venezuela's Orinoco oil sands (the largest undeveloped crude deposit on the planet) would require on the order of $100 billion, and argues the economically optimal design would site roughly 5 gigawatts of nuclear reactors on top of the project, since a single 1-gigawatt reactor throws off about $250 million a year of waste steam heat that is highly valuable for injecting into heavy-oil reservoirs to reduce viscosity — implying roughly $1.25 billion a year in cash flow from the waste-steam byproduct alone, though the reactors themselves would cost an additional $30-35 billion.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A novel nuclear-plus-heavy-oil co-location framework that could apply beyond Venezuela to any large heavy-oil/oil-sands development, and a reminder that Orinoco development is not investable at scale until Venezuelan political and social stability improves.
insights.quote: it is anticipated that one a one gawatt reactor generates uh $250 million worth of waste steam a year... the waste product would generate $1.25 billion a year in cash flow.

insights.claim: Rule says the 'easy money' in uranium was made years ago when uranium traded below the cost of production; the 'certain money' lies ahead, since companies that lost money at $20-40/lb are now profitable at $85-90/lb, yet that price still isn't high enough to incentivize much new supply even as demand keeps growing rapidly.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Reframes uranium bulls' expectations: the trade has shifted from a deep-value/mispricing bet to a supply-response bet, implying continued price upside is needed to draw out new production.
insights.quote: companies that made no money whatsoever at $40 a pound uranium... are making real good money at $85 and $90 a pound. But $85 or $90 a pound doesn't seem to be enough to incent very much new production.

insights.claim: Rule argues the resumed US-Iran conflict reinforces a global energy-security imperative that only nuclear power (via uranium) can satisfy, drawing a direct historical parallel to the 1973 Arab oil embargo, which drove France to build the world's fourth-largest nuclear fleet and Japan the third-largest.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Positions geopolitical conflict as a structural, multi-decade demand driver for uranium and nuclear buildouts, not just an oil-market story.
insights.quote: it was the 1973 Arab oil embargo that caused the production of the French nuclear fleet, the fourth largest in the world, and caused the construction of the Japanese nuclear fleet, the third largest in the world.

insights.claim: Rule cites Japan's own assessment that uranium is dense enough that a single warehouse of the fuel can power the entire country for five years — an energy-security density argument that coal, gas, or battery storage cannot match.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A concrete, quotable data point for the strategic-reserve/energy-security case for nuclear power over other generation sources.
insights.quote: uranium is a dense enough fuel that one warehouse can contain enough material to power Japan for 5 years.

insights.claim: For uranium exposure, Rule ranks options by risk: the Sprott Physical Uranium Trust (SPUT, where he discloses he is the largest shareholder) or a uranium ETF for lower risk; Cameco (largest Western producer) or Kazatomprom (Kazakh competitor) for producers; and a junior basket of NexGen, Paladin, and potentially Denison for those willing to take on more volatility and news-flow risk.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A full risk-tiered uranium-investment menu, with an explicit conflict-of-interest disclosure on the largest recommended vehicle.

insights.claim: Rule contrasts the last-built US gigawatt nuclear reactor, which cost about $29 billion including delays and customization, with China's ability to build gigawatt reactors for about $6 billion each by repeatedly deploying a single standardized design without local political customization.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cost gap a standardized US reactor design and streamlined permitting could close, a specific policy lever for the domestic nuclear renaissance.
insights.quote: the Chinese are building gigawatt reactors for $6 billion each... They aren't required to be re-engineered for local political preference.

insights.claim: Rule proposes that US nuclear costs could fall dramatically if the tax code allowed 5-year depreciation on plant construction (as in China, Sweden, and Denmark) instead of the current 30-year straight-line depreciation, arguing this single change would eliminate most of the US cost disadvantage versus these countries.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A concrete, actionable policy proposal investors can watch for as a leading indicator of whether the US nuclear buildout will actually reach Chinese-level cost efficiency.
insights.quote: we could depreciate uh for tax purposes in 5 years, including against other income. In the United States, we would depreciate that via straight line for 30 years.

themes.theme: Government money in critical minerals: taxpayer horror, investor delight

insights.claim: Rule holds a deliberately dual view on government subsidies flooding into critical minerals and nuclear: as a taxpayer he calls the spending horrifying and certain to be misallocated based on political vote-generation rather than risk-adjusted return, but as an investor he calls the resulting 'dumb money' inflow attractive because it lifts asset prices ahead of him.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A clear framework for separating policy judgment from investment positioning — fade the politics, front-run the capital flow.
insights.quote: the idea that a bunch of dumb money comes behind me and there's no money as dumb as government money uh is attractive.

insights.claim: Rule cites Mountain Pass (the US rare-earth mine in California) as receiving a large government grant despite having gone bankrupt three times within his lifetime, as an example of politically motivated capital allocation overriding a poor underlying investment track record.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable example of subsidy-driven capital going to a historically troubled asset — a caution for investors chasing government-backed critical-minerals names purely on policy momentum.
insights.quote: Mountain Pass, as an example, uh in our former domicile, California, uh received a massive government grant. Uh in my lifetime, that deposit has been bankrupt three times.

insights.claim: Rule notes that gold-mining construction loans for non-investment-grade juniors (e.g., Aris Mining) typically cost 13-15% per annum, versus about 6.75% for investment-grade companies borrowing on balance sheet, versus roughly 3.5% for Chinese state-linked miners like Zijin borrowing through the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
entities: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China
insights.so_what: Quantifies a structural cost-of-capital disadvantage (roughly 4x) facing Western junior miners versus Chinese state-backed competitors, a key reason Chinese mining companies can out-invest and out-scale Western juniors over time.
insights.quote: Zjin's cost of capital is 3 and a half%... their cost of capital for construction is somewhere between 13 and 15%.

insights.claim: Rule reports growing conference-floor interest in previously niche critical minerals — antimony, titanium, and tungsten — driven by deglobalization and countries seeking supply chains from safer jurisdictions, alongside continued strong interest in copper.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule / Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Signals broadening investor attention beyond copper into a wider basket of supply-constrained strategic minerals, worth tracking for early positioning.

insights.claim: Rule warns that smaller, more obscure mineral markets (vanadium, molybdenum, antimony, tungsten) offer greater leveraged upside but also much higher volatility, illustrated by the molybdenum market roughly 15 years ago, where a supply squeeze led major copper porphyry producers to add molybdenum circuits to their plants, flipping the market from a shortage to an oversupply and crashing the price.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: A cautionary historical precedent for anyone chasing the current small-cap critical-minerals enthusiasm — niche mineral shortages can reverse quickly once producers respond.

themes.theme: North Sea, gold, and closing macro views

insights.claim: Rule sees real geological upside in the UK North Sea given existing producing infrastructure, and speculates the UK's poor fiscal position could push its government to reopen serious North Sea exploration, noting the contrast with Norway's roughly $3 trillion sovereign wealth fund built from the same basin.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Flags a potential policy-driven reopening of a mature, infrastructure-rich basin as an emerging opportunity to watch, contingent on UK political will.
insights.quote: I wonder if the average British citizen isn't looking across the North Sea at Norway and wondering why the Norwegians have a $3 trillion sovereign wealth fund and the Brits can't balance the budget.

insights.claim: Rule notes the Lundin family discovered a 2-billion-barrel field in Norway in an area previously thought geologically mature, evidence that the North Sea (including the UK side, which hasn't seen concerted modern exploration in two decades) still holds significant undiscovered resource.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that mature basins are fully explored, supporting the North Sea reopening thesis with a concrete precedent.

insights.claim: Rule has no directional view on whether precious metals have bottomed, saying it depends entirely on the path of US interest rates, but predicts that if an economic slowdown prompts the government to increase artificial liquidity and cut rates, gold could rally on the order of magnitude seen in late 1975.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: Ties the next major gold leg explicitly to a rate-cutting response to economic weakness rather than to the current geopolitical or inflation narrative, giving investors a specific macro trigger to watch.
insights.quote: if we have any kind of economic slowdown... the political response will be to increase artificial liquidity in the US economy and lower the interest rates... I think you'll see gold go on a tear... in the order of magnitude as late 1975.

insights.claim: Rule's BattleBank, focused on sound-money and precious-metals-oriented customers, was about 10-11 weeks into general operations, holding roughly $130 million in deposits, adding about $1 million/day in new deposits and about $250,000/day in gold deposits.
insights.speaker: Rick Rule
insights.so_what: An operational growth data point for a niche financial-services venture tied to the broader precious-metals/sound-money investor community Rule serves.
insights.quote: we're raising about a million dollars a day in new deposits... We're at about $130 million in deposits.
